At a glance

Best months
  • Late March to May for displaying bustards and full song
  • October for the crane roosts and Helgoland
  • November to February for geese and eagles
Regions
The Wadden Sea and Schleswig-HolsteinHelgolandThe Darss, the Bodden and RuegenThe Mecklenburg Lake DistrictThe Lower Oder valley and the UckermarkBrandenburg: the Havelland, Linum and the bustard fieldsThe Lusatian ponds and Upper LusatiaThe HarzThe Lower Saxony moors and the DuemmerThe Upper Rhine and the KaiserstuhlThe Bavarian ForestThe Bavarian Alps and the Alpine lakes
Itineraries
The Lusatian Ponds4 daysHelgoland in Autumn5 daysThe Mecklenburg Lakes5 daysThe Upper Rhine and the Kaiserstuhl5 daysThe Crane Fortnight7 daysBerlin and Brandenburg8 daysThe Northern Coasts8 daysThe Southern Forests9 days
Getting around
A hire car is the honest answer for most of the twelve regions, but Germany is the easiest country on this site to bird by train, with the ICE reaching Rostock, Berlin, Freiburg and Munich, regional services most of the rest, and a ferry to Helgoland.

When to Go

Germany is twelve regions in three landscapes, so the right month depends far more on where you go than on the year as a whole. The strip below is a national view; each region card says what its own season is.

Spring

March to June

Bustards display on the Brandenburg fields from late March, the Wadden Sea fills with passage waders, and by June the mountain and forest regions are open and singing.

Go for Displaying bustards, full forest song, and the widest choice of regions in the year.

Trade off The Alpine and Bavarian Forest tops hold snow into May, so an early mountain trip is a valley trip.

Typical daily average
  • the Baltic coast: 0 to 19 °C / 32 to 66 °F
  • Brandenburg: 1 to 22 °C / 34 to 72 °F
  • the Upper Rhine: 2 to 23 °C / 36 to 73 °F
  • the Bavarian Alps: -1 to 20 °C / 30 to 68 °F

Autumn

July to October

The crane year decides the German autumn. Birds gather on the Bodden from late September and on the Linum ponds and the Diepholz moors through October, and Helgoland takes whatever the North Sea blows in.

Go for The largest crane gathering in western Europe, and the best fortnight of the year on Helgoland.

Trade off The cranes bring crowds, and the Zingst viewing points are managed with access limits in season.

Typical daily average
  • the Baltic coast: 7 to 21 °C / 45 to 70 °F
  • Brandenburg: 6 to 24 °C / 43 to 75 °F
  • the Upper Rhine: 6 to 25 °C / 43 to 77 °F
  • the Bavarian Alps: 4 to 22 °C / 39 to 72 °F

Winter

November to February

Geese and diving duck fill the Baltic bays and the Havel and Oder floodplains, and White-tailed Eagle is at its easiest of the year over open water.

Go for Eagles, six-figure goose flocks, and the cheapest rooms of the year.

Trade off Eight hours of daylight, and the mountain and forest regions are effectively shut.

Typical daily average
  • the Baltic coast: -2 to 7 °C / 28 to 45 °F
  • Brandenburg: -2 to 7 °C / 28 to 45 °F
  • the Upper Rhine: -1 to 9 °C / 30 to 48 °F
  • the Bavarian Alps: -5 to 6 °C / 23 to 43 °F

The Southern Forests

Munich (MUC), the Bavarian Forest, the Bavarian Alps

Deadwood forest for woodpeckers and owls, then the Alps for Wallcreeper and Ptarmigan, with the Chiemsee delta on the way between. June to September, once the high ground is open.

The Wadden Sea and Schleswig-Holstein

Tidal flat, salt marsh and halligen on the North Sea coast, an hour and a half from Hamburg

The German Wadden Sea is a national park and a World Heritage site, and it works the way the Dutch and Danish stretches do: the tide decides the day, and high water pushes waders onto roosts you can watch from a dike. Autumn passage here is counted in millions of birds.

  • Habitat: The German share of the Wadden Sea runs north from the Elbe estuary to the Danish border. It is intertidal mud, sandbank and grazed saltmarsh behind sea walls, and the Eider barrage closes the one large river mouth along it.
  • When: Autumn passage carries the weight, when up to 1.8 million waterfowl and waders use the Wadden Sea. Up to 100,000 Common Shelduck moult in the German section from mid-July to September, and the Lapland reintroduction scheme's Lesser White-fronted Geese stage here.
  • Getting there: Katinger Watt lies behind the Eidersperrwerk barrage at the mouth of the Eider and is the place to try for the staging geese and for Broad-billed Sandpiper.
  • Look for: Red Knot, Bar-tailed Godwit, Eurasian Spoonbill, Common Shelduck, Kentish Plover, Barnacle Goose
  • National park: Schleswig-Holstein Wadden Sea National Park
  • Stops:
    • : Salt marsh and the most photographed lighthouse in Germany. A track leads out from the car park, with waders on the marsh and geese in winter.
    • : A large diked lagoon south of Husum, with tracks and screens. It is one of the best single wader sites on the German coast.
    • : A polder (land reclaimed from the sea behind a dike) with young woodland at the Eider mouth. It has hides and a nature centre.
    • : Two shallow lakes behind the sea wall north of Husum. Watch from the dike road for duck, waders and roosting geese.
    • : A brackish basin on Sylt with a path around it, and the island's best wader and duck site.
    • : Reserve, lagoon and dike south of Meldorf, with towers over the flats.
  • Visitor centres: Multimar Wattforum, Toenning
  • Also covers: Beltringharder Koog, Friedrichskoog, Hauke-Haien-Koog, Husum, Katinger Watt, List auf Sylt, Multimar Wattforum, Toenning, Rantumbecken, Sylt, Sankt Peter-Ording, Schleswig-Holstein Wadden Sea National Park, Speicherkoog Dithmarschen, Westerhever lighthouse and salt marsh
  • Also watch for: Harbour and grey seals haul out on the sandbanks, and harbour porpoise are regular off Sylt in summer.

Helgoland

A red sandstone island 50 km out in the German Bight, by ferry from Cuxhaven or Buesum

Germany's only offshore island is its seabird cliff and its rarity trap in one. Gannets and auks nest on the Lummenfelsen, which is the smallest nature reserve in Germany, and the gardens and fields of the Oberland take whatever the wind brings in spring and autumn.

  • Habitat: Two small islands 50 km out in the North Sea. Oberland carries the cliffs, the observatory and what cover there is, and the low sandy Dune beside it takes the passage waders.
  • When: Spring and autumn passage, and the island's 400-species list is built on them. Thrush Nightingale comes through in spring, and Yellow-browed Warbler, Richard's Pipit and Little and Rustic Buntings in autumn. A single May day in 1996 produced 135 species.
  • Getting there: The bird observatory sits on Oberland and takes the majority of migrants. Dune is a beach resort and still worth walking for shorebirds.
  • Look for: Northern Gannet, Common Murre, Razorbill, Black-legged Kittiwake, Northern Fulmar, Bluethroat
  • Parks and reserves: Lummenfelsen nature reserve
  • Stops:
    • : The seabird cliff on the west side. A made path runs along the top, and Guillemots, Razorbills, Kittiwakes and the gannet colony nest below it.
    • : The free-standing sea stack at the northern tip, at the end of the cliff path and the densest part of the colony.
    • Helgoland Bird Observatory : The ringing station in the Oberland. It has run since 1910 and has a trapping garden and a visitor centre.
    • : The sand island a short ferry hop away, with the seal colony and passage waders on the beaches.
    • : The plateau of gardens, fields and scrub where migrants land. The island's paths cross it.
  • Visitor centres: Vogelwarte Helgoland
  • Also covers: Helgoland Bird Observatory, Helgoland Duene, Lange Anna, Lummenfelsen nature reserve, Oberland, Vogelwarte Helgoland
  • Also watch for: Grey seals pup on the neighbouring dune island from November, in the open and at close range, which happens almost nowhere else in Europe.

The Darss, the Bodden and Ruegen

Shallow Baltic lagoon, pine forest and chalk cliff, three hours north of Berlin

The autumn crane gathering on the Bodden shallows is the largest in western Europe, and Pramort at the tip of the Zingst peninsula is where it is watched. The same coast holds White-tailed Eagle all year and the chalk cliffs of Jasmund on Ruegen an hour to the east.

  • Habitat: Shallow brackish lagoons, called Bodden here, lie between the Baltic and a chain of low sandy peninsulas and islands. Reed fringes and grazed coastal grassland stand behind them.
  • When: Autumn. Up to 40,000 Common Cranes pass through and stop at traditional roosts, and a September day on Ruegen can produce over a hundred species including White-tailed Eagle, Broad-billed Sandpiper, Caspian Tern and Aquatic Warbler.
  • Getting there: Udarser Wiek is one of the traditional crane stops and is visible from the east side of Ummanz, a quiet off-island also reached through Gingst.
  • Look for: Common Crane, White-tailed Eagle, Greylag Goose, Tundra Bean Goose, Common Goldeneye, Black Woodpecker
  • National parks:
    • Vorpommersche Boddenlandschaft National Park
    • Jasmund National Park, Beech forest on the chalk cliffs of northern Ruegen, with the Koenigsstuhl viewpoint and Peregrines on the face.
  • Stops:
    • : The viewing platform at the eastern tip of the Zingst, on foot or by bike. The crane roost is watched from here, and access is managed in season.
    • Kranorama Guentershagen : A purpose-built crane hide over a feeding field south of the Bodden, staffed in autumn.
    • : A sandbank island in the Bodden and the core of the crane roost. Watch it from the shore rather than entering.
    • : The wooded north-western tip of the Darss, with a lighthouse, a nature centre and passage along the shore.
    • : A grassy headland on the Moenchgut peninsula, with wide views over the Baltic and the Bodden.
  • Visitor centres: Kranich-Informationszentrum, Guentershagen
  • Also covers: Barth, Bock island, Born a. Darss, Darsser Ort, Grosser Zicker, Ruegen, Jasmund National Park, Kranich-Informationszentrum, Guentershagen, Kranorama Guentershagen, Pramort, Prerow, Sassnitz, Vorpommersche Boddenlandschaft National Park, Zingst
  • Also watch for: Red deer rut in the Darss forest through October, at the same time as the cranes, and the two are usually sold as one trip.

The Mecklenburg Lake District

Lake, bog and beech forest, an hour and a half north of Berlin

The Mueritz National Park protects the biggest lake wholly inside Germany and the bog and beech country around it. This is the easiest place in the country for White-tailed Eagle and Osprey over the same water, and the beech stands are part of a World Heritage listing.

  • Habitat: Lowland lakeland between Berlin and the Baltic at Rostock. It mixes large shallow lakes and fish ponds with wet grassland and forest, and holds about 150 breeding species.
  • When: The breeding season, for White-tailed Eagle, Lesser Spotted Eagle and Common Crane. Cranes roost on the lakes through autumn.
  • Getting there: Lewitzer Teiche and its surrounding grassland lie east of Parchim and are the best of it. Cranes roost on the two lakes by the Goldberg to Crivitz road near Langenhagen, also east of Parchim.
  • Look for: White-tailed Eagle, Osprey, Common Crane, Black Stork, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Red Kite
  • National park:
    • Mueritz National Park, The park itself. Marked cycle routes and a shuttle bus cross it, and forest and bog ring the lake's eastern shore.
  • Stops:
    • : A village with a staffed eagle observation point and a camera on a nearby nest, run by the park.
    • : A shallow park lake with an observation tower over the reed. A footpath reaches it.
    • : The town end of the lake, with boat trips out onto the water and duck on it in winter.
    • : The World Heritage beech stand in the park's eastern section, walked on marked paths.
  • Visitor centres: Nationalpark-Information Federow
  • Also covers: Federow eagle hide, Mueritz lakeshore at Waren, Mueritz National Park, Nationalpark-Information Federow, Neustrelitz, Roebel, Serrahn beech forest, Specker See, Waren (Mueritz)
  • Also watch for: Otter and beaver are both established on the lake system, and red deer rut in the park's forest in autumn.

The Lower Oder valley and the Uckermark

River floodplain on the Polish border, an hour and a half north-east of Berlin

Germany's only floodplain national park runs along the Oder, and the polders flood in winter by design. Cranes and geese stage here in tens of thousands, Aquatic Warbler still turns up in the sedge, and the Uckermark behind it is quiet farmland with more Red Kite than anywhere else in Europe.

  • Habitat: A floodplain running 180 km along the Polish border. It holds wet meadow, oxbow and reed, with the sedge marshes that carry Aquatic Warbler.
  • When: The breeding season for Corn Crake, Little Crake and the 10 to 20 pairs of Aquatic Warbler, with Black and White Storks, White-tailed and Lesser Spotted Eagles and Common Crane alongside them. Winter brings as many as 200 Smew, with Whooper and Bewick's Swans and Rough-legged Buzzard.
  • Getting there: Schwedt sits halfway along the valley about 100 km north-east of Berlin and is the base for it.
  • Look for: Common Crane, White-tailed Eagle, Red Kite, Black Stork, Tundra Bean Goose, Whooper Swan
  • National park:
    • Lower Oder Valley National Park, The floodplain park itself. Dike paths run between Criewen and Gartz, and the polders flood from November.
  • Stops:
    • : The park's headquarters village, with a visitor centre and the start of the dike walks.
    • : A bluff above the valley, with a tower giving the overview of the polders.
    • : The northern polders, the quietest part of the park and the best of the goose ground.
    • Blumberger Muehle : A NABU nature centre in old fish ponds south-west of the park, with trails and hides.
  • Visitor centres: NABU Blumberger Muehle
  • Also covers: Angermuende, Criewen, Gartz polder, Lower Oder Valley National Park, NABU Blumberger Muehle, Schwedt, Stuetzkow viewpoint
  • Also watch for: Beaver work the whole floodplain and are easy to find at dusk, and elk cross from Poland from time to time.

Brandenburg: the Havelland, Linum and the bustard fields

Flat farmland, wet meadow and crane roost around Berlin, under an hour from the city

The country an hour west and north of Berlin does three things at once. Great Bustard came within a few dozen birds of vanishing from Germany and hold on here behind predator fencing, with hides anyone can use. The Linum ponds and the Rhinluch take one of the largest crane roosts in the country every October. And the Havel wet meadows and the open fields between them carry a breeding wader list that has gone from most of lowland Europe.

  • Habitat: Marsh, grassland and forest spread across the lowlands around Berlin, with fish pond complexes and the steppe-like open fields that still hold Great Bustard.
  • When: The breeding season, for Great Bustard and Great Snipe on the open grassland and White-tailed Eagle over the marshes. Osprey and Red Kite are still regular less than an hour by train from Berlin.
  • Getting there: Havellaendisches Luch lies 70 km west of Berlin, between the towns of Nauen and Rathenow, and the bustard grassland centres on Garlitz. Two tower hides look out over the best of it. Guelper See lies a little further north and holds good birding of its own.
  • Look for: Great Bustard, Common Crane, Montagu's Harrier, Red Kite, Whinchat, Eurasian Curlew
  • Parks and reserves: Westhavelland Nature Park, Naturpark Nuthe-Nieplitz (nature park)
  • Stops:
    • : The largest of the three bustard areas, with a staffed viewing hide reached from Buckow bei Nennhausen. It is best from March to May, when the males display.
    • : The southern bustard area, wet meadow with a tower, and the strongest ground in Germany for Montagu's Harrier.
    • : Old carp ponds beside the village of Linum, and the assembly point for the Rhinluch crane roost. Signed viewpoints and a staffed information hut run through October.
    • : The fen basin the Linum cranes roost in. Watch it at dawn and dusk from the dike roads rather than entering.
    • : A shallow lake in the lower Havel, a nature reserve. Geese, duck and White-tailed Eagle use it through the winter.
    • : The Havel floodplain downstream of Rathenow, the largest river restoration project in Europe. Watch it from the dike roads around Gulpe.
  • Visitor centres: Naturparkzentrum Westhavelland, Milow
  • Also covers: Bad Belzig, Belziger Landschaftswiesen, Brandenburg an der Havel, Gulper See, Havellaendisches Luch, Linumer Teiche, Naturpark Nuthe-Nieplitz, Naturparkzentrum Westhavelland, Milow, Nennhausen, Rathenow, Rhinluch, The lower Havel at Gulpe, Westhavelland Nature Park
  • Also watch for: The bustard areas are grazed and mown late for the birds, which makes them good for orchids and for brown hare. The Westhavelland is Germany's first International Dark Sky Reserve, so the crane roost at dusk comes with a real night sky.

The Lusatian ponds and Upper Lusatia

Eight hundred years of fish ponds in eastern Saxony, two hours south-east of Berlin

Carp have been farmed here since the Middle Ages, and the ponds they made are now a UNESCO biosphere reserve holding one of the densest concentrations of breeding waterbirds in Germany. Bittern, Little Bittern and Black Stork all nest, and the ponds are drained in autumn, which concentrates everything.

  • Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Black Stork, White-tailed Eagle, Whiskered Tern, Red-crested Pochard, Bluethroat
  • Parks and reserves: Oberlausitzer Heide- und Teichlandschaft Biosphere Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : The biosphere reserve itself. Marked paths and dams run between the ponds.
    • : A pond group east of Bautzen, with a nature trail and screens. It is the easiest bittern site in the reserve.
    • : The northern ponds near Kreba-Neudorf. They are quieter, with a tower over the largest water.
    • Haus der Tausend Teiche : The reserve's visitor centre at Wartha, with a trail out into the ponds.
    • : A large reservoir north of Niesky. It is drawn down in autumn, with roosting geese and cranes.
  • Visitor centres: Haus der Tausend Teiche, Wartha
  • Also covers: Bautzen, Guttauer Teiche, Haus der Tausend Teiche, Wartha, Hoyerswerda, Kreba-Neudorf, Niederspreer Teichgebiet, Niesky, Oberlausitzer Heide- und Teichlandschaft Biosphere Reserve, Talsperre Quitzdorf
  • Also watch for: Wolves recolonised Germany through this landscape in 2000, and otter are common on the pond system.

The Harz

Spruce and beech uplands in the middle of the country, two hours from Hanover

The Harz is the northernmost range in Germany with a subalpine top, and its national park has a Black Stork density that few places match. Lynx were released here from 2000 and are now breeding. The Brocken plateau carries Ring Ouzel and Water Pipit at a latitude that has no business holding them.

  • Look for: Black Stork, Ring Ouzel, Water Pipit, Eurasian Pygmy Owl, Black Woodpecker, Peregrine Falcon
  • National park:
    • Harz National Park, The park across two states. Marked trails and a narrow-gauge railway cross it.
  • Stops:
    • : The highest point in northern Germany, on foot from Torfhaus or by steam railway, with subalpine heath on top.
    • : An eighteenth-century reservoir on the plateau, with bog and spruce around it and a path along the shore.
    • : A large reservoir on the eastern side, with wooded valleys. Black Stork cross the water.
    • : The lynx enclosure and crag viewpoint above Bad Harzburg, with Peregrine on the rock.
  • Visitor centres: Nationalpark-Besucherzentrum TorfHaus
  • Also covers: Bad Harzburg, Brocken, Harz National Park, Luchsgehege Rabenklippe, Nationalpark-Besucherzentrum TorfHaus, Oderteich, Rappbodetalsperre, Sankt Andreasberg, Wernigerode
  • Also watch for: Lynx are established and occasionally seen from the trails, and the Harz has the largest wildcat population in Germany.

The Lower Saxony moors and the Duemmer

Raised bog, wet meadow and a shallow lake west of Hanover

The Diepholz moors are cut-over raised bog under restoration, and the crane roost that has built up on them is the largest in western Germany after the Baltic. This is Lower Saxony's answer to the Bodden, an hour west of Hanover. The Duemmer, a shallow lake with wet grassland around it, sits half an hour away and answers for waders and marsh birds.

  • When: Good all year. Common Crane and Bluethroat hold the ground through the year. Black-tailed Godwit is here from March to August.
  • Look for: Common Crane, Black-tailed Godwit, Eurasian Bittern, Montagu's Harrier, European Nightjar, Bluethroat
  • Parks and reserves: Duemmer Nature Park
  • Stops:
    • : The chain of restored bogs between Diepholz and Wagenfeld, with signed crane viewpoints used from October.
    • : One of the largest bogs in the chain, with a boardwalk and a tower over the roost.
    • : A shallow lake with reed and wet grassland on its southern shore. Watch from the dike and a tower.
    • : Restored wet grassland at the south end of the Duemmer, and the best breeding wader ground in the region.
    • : A bog west of Diepholz, with a viewing tower and a crane roost of its own.
  • Visitor centres: Naturschutzring Duemmer, Huede
  • Also covers: Diepholzer Moorniederung, Duemmer Nature Park, Lembruch, Naturschutzring Duemmer, Huede, Neustaedter Moor, Ochsenmoor, Rehdener Geestmoor, Vechta, Wagenfeld
  • Also watch for: The restored bogs carry adder and a strong dragonfly list, and the moor tracks are good for roe deer at dusk.

The Upper Rhine and the Kaiserstuhl

River floodplain and a volcanic hill of vineyards, south-west on the French border

The Kaiserstuhl is the warmest corner of Germany, and its terraced vineyards and loess hollows carry Hoopoe, Bee-eater and Wryneck in numbers found nowhere else in the country. The Rhine floodplain forest either side of it is a different habitat again, with the German woodpecker list close to complete.

  • Habitat: Oxbow lake and remnant oak floodplain woodland in the Rhine valley between Frankfurt and Mannheim, with gravel pits worked into the terrace behind. The Kuhkopf reserve alone carries over 100 breeding species.
  • When: The breeding season for Red-necked Grebe, Corn Crake, Black Woodpecker and White-spotted Bluethroat, and passage for the shorebirds on the pits and the shallow margins.
  • Getting there: Leave the autobahn west to Gernsheim and turn north on Route 44 towards Riedstadt, then continue through Biebesheim to Stockstadt. Take the first road west and park in Riedstadt-Erfelden, where a loop trail runs round the oxbow lake. The gravel pits on the minor road west of Biebesheim are worth checking on the way.
  • Look for: Common Hoopoe, European Bee-eater, Eurasian Wryneck, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Black Kite, Grey-headed Woodpecker
  • Parks and reserves: Kuehkopf-Knoblochsaue nature reserve, Suedschwarzwald Nature Park
  • Stops:
    • : The volcanic hill west of Freiburg. Watch from the vineyard tracks and the loess hollow paths above Ihringen and Vogtsburg.
    • : Floodplain forest and old river channels along the Rhine, on marked paths from the town.
    • : The largest nature reserve in Hesse, an old Rhine meander cut off in 1829. It has floodplain forest, meadow and a visitor centre.
    • : A reserve of Rhine side channels and wet forest south of Kehl. Walk it or paddle it.
    • : A dry hill at the Kaiserstuhl's western edge above the Rhine, with a nature trail through steppe grassland.
  • Visitor centres: Umweltbildungszentrum Schatzinsel Kuehkopf
  • Also covers: Badische Rheinauen at Breisach, Breisach am Rhein, Ihringen, Kehl, Kuehkopf-Knoblochsaue nature reserve, Limburg, Sasbach, Riedstadt, Suedschwarzwald Nature Park, Taubergiessen, Umweltbildungszentrum Schatzinsel Kuehkopf, Vogtsburg im Kaiserstuhl
  • Also watch for: The Kaiserstuhl is the richest orchid ground in Germany and carries praying mantis and European green lizard on the same slopes.

The Bavarian Forest

Old spruce and beech forest on the Czech border, two hours north-east of Munich

The oldest national park in Germany, and the one run on a policy of leaving the forest alone. Bark beetle killed a great deal of the spruce and the standing deadwood that followed is why the woodpecker and owl list here is the best in the country. Capercaillie still hold on at altitude.

  • Habitat: Beech and coniferous forest covering 130 square kilometres along the Czech border in south-east Bavaria, with standing deadwood enough to carry four woodpeckers and three owls.
  • When: Spring and early summer for Hazel Grouse, Eurasian Pygmy-Owl, Tengmalm's Owl and White-backed, Three-toed and Black Woodpeckers. March is the easier month for woodpeckers anywhere in Germany.
  • Getting there: The park visitor centre is at Neuschoenau. Spiegelau sits at the south-west corner about 40 km north of Passau and is the best base. Gfall lies 6 km north of Spiegelau on the way to Rachel, Flanitzbene north of Spiegelau via Althuette, and Zwieslerwaldhaus 15 km north of Zwiesel for White-backed Woodpecker.
  • Look for: Western Capercaillie, Eurasian Pygmy Owl, Boreal Owl, Eurasian Three-toed Woodpecker, White-backed Woodpecker, Hazel Grouse
  • National park:
    • Bavarian Forest National Park, The park itself, a network of marked trails with a free shuttle bus between the trailheads.
  • Stops:
    • : One of the two high summits, walked from Spiegelau through spruce forest into the summit zone. Three-toed Woodpecker work the deadwood.
    • : The other summit, above Neuschoenau. A long stretch of standing dead spruce makes it the best owl and woodpecker ground in the park.
    • Hans-Eisenmann-Haus : The park's main visitor centre, with the treetop walkway and the animal enclosures beside it.
    • : A glacial lake under the Arber, with a floating bog and a path around it.
  • Visitor centres: Hans-Eisenmann-Haus, Neuschoenau
  • Also covers: Bavarian Forest National Park, Bayerisch Eisenstein, Grafenau, Grosser Arbersee, Hans-Eisenmann-Haus, Neuschoenau, Lusen, Rachel, Zwiesel
  • Also watch for: Lynx are established and occasionally seen, and the park's animal enclosures hold wolf, lynx and bison for visitors who will not meet them wild.

The Bavarian Alps and the Alpine lakes

Alpine rock, mountain forest and shallow foothill lakes, an hour south of Munich

Germany's only alpine national park is at Berchtesgaden, and a cable car or a valley walk reaches Wallcreeper, Alpine Accentor and Rock Ptarmigan without a mountaineering day. The shallow lakes on the foothill plain below, Chiemsee and Ammersee, are the country's best inland waterbird sites in winter.

  • Habitat: Alpine rock, coniferous forest and summer pasture holding Germany's highest ground, 2,713 m at Watzmann in Berchtesgaden and 2,966 m at Zugspitze, with the Inn dams and the Bodensee marshes lying at their feet.
  • When: Summer and autumn for the high tops, which stay shut until mid-June at the earliest and open again when the mountain roads clear. Rock Ptarmigan, White-winged Snowfinch, Alpine Accentor and Yellow-billed Chough are the reason to go up.
  • Getting there: There are visitor centres at Berchtesgaden and Koenigssee, and Eurasian Pygmy-Owl is above the Hintersee, south-west of Ramsau. Garmisch-Partenkirchen is 90 km south of Munich on Autobahn 95, with a cable car and rack railway up Zugspitze and a second cable car to Hochalm at 1,700 m for Alpine Accentor and Citril Finch.
  • Look for: Wallcreeper, Alpine Accentor, Rock Ptarmigan, Golden Eagle, Black Woodpecker, Red-crested Pochard
  • National park:
    • Berchtesgaden National Park, The alpine park around the Koenigssee. Watch from the boat, the Jenner cable car and the valley paths.
  • Stops:
    • : The fjord lake at the park's heart, crossed by electric boat, with cliffs either side.
    • : The river delta at the south end of the Chiemsee, a reserve with towers and the best waterbird site in Bavaria.
    • : Reed and wet meadow at the lake's southern end, with a tower and marked paths.
    • : The limestone range on the Austrian border. The Karwendelbahn climbs from Mittenwald, and alpine ground starts straight off the top station.
    • : The largest intact bog in central Europe, on the plain below the Alps, with a circular boardwalk.
  • Visitor centres: Haus der Berge, Berchtesgaden
  • Also covers: Ammersee south shore, Berchtesgaden National Park, Chiemsee and the Achendelta, Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Haus der Berge, Berchtesgaden, Herrsching am Ammersee, Karwendel at Mittenwald, Koenigssee, Murnauer Moos, Seebruck
  • Also watch for: Ibex, chamois and marmot all live in the Berchtesgaden park, and the Alpine Salamander comes out on wet paths.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Germany?

October, if you want the single best thing the country does: the crane gathering on the Bodden, at Linum and on the Diepholz moors, all at once, with Helgoland taking migrants at the same time. Late March to May for displaying Great Bustards and full forest song. November to February for geese and White-tailed Eagle.

Where should I go for a first German birding trip?

Berlin and Brandenburg. Great Bustards an hour west of the city, the Linum crane roost an hour north, and the Oder floodplain an hour further on, all from one base with an airport attached. The German routes here are built on exactly this ground.

Do I need a car?

Less than anywhere else on this site. The ICE reaches Rostock, Berlin, Freiburg and Munich in a few hours and regional trains reach most of the rest, and the Bavarian Forest park runs a free shuttle between its trailheads. A car still helps for the Havelland bustard hides, the Lusatian ponds and the Diepholz moors, where rural bus services are thin. Helgoland is reached by ferry from Cuxhaven or Buesum.

Where do I see Great Bustard in Germany?

Three protected areas, all in Brandenburg and Saxony-Anhalt, all with hides open to anyone. The Havellaendisches Luch is the largest, and Buckow bei Nennhausen is the way in. The Belziger Landschaftswiesen to the south is the second, and the best ground in the country for Montagu's Harrier at the same time. Late March to May for display.

Is Helgoland worth the journey?

In late September and October, yes, and it is the only German seabird cliff at any time of year. The island is fifty kilometres out, so it takes whatever the North Sea blows in, and the observatory has been ringing there since 1910. Stay over rather than day-tripping: the day boat gives you about four hours.

Which German birds are hard to find anywhere else in western Europe?

The Bavarian Forest carries Three-toed and White-backed Woodpecker, Pygmy and Boreal Owl and Hazel Grouse in one park, on standing deadwood the park deliberately left after a bark beetle outbreak. Great Bustard is the other: the German population is one of only a handful left in western Europe.

How many crane species are there, and how many can I see?

One in Germany, the Common Crane, and it arrives in six figures. The Bodden roost behind the Darss is the largest gathering in western Europe, and Linum and the Diepholz moors take the inland birds.

How much does a German birding trip cost?

Accommodation is the largest line and Germany is a mid-priced European country for it. A guided operator week runs to several thousand dollars; the same ground self-driven or by train costs a fraction of that, and almost every reserve above is free to enter.

Are the certified places to stay above good for birds?

A certificate says a property was audited against a checklist, not that it is good for birding, and this guide never treats it as such. GreenSign is the one partial exception: it audits and publishes a biodiversity score out of 100, which is shown on the card where the register gives one.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Sites on this page differ from each other more than any rating could carry, so this is the framework the standard British guides use, and the reserve's own page and warden hold the answers.

  • Permission · some reserves open ground to disabled visitors that is closed to everyone else, and it is granted by asking.
  • Priority · parking bays, hides and the nearest paths are often held for disabled visitors. Ask what is reserved and how to claim it.
  • Parking · how close a car reaches the birds shapes the whole day. Ring ahead for the nearest hard standing to the water or the hide.
  • Paths · surfaces, gradients and gate widths vary inside a single reserve. Ask which trail is boarded, surfaced or level.
  • Perches · a hide with a low window, or a bench where the view opens, turns a viewpoint into a morning.

Every reserve above with its own link carries its access detail there, and a warden answers what a page cannot.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, Germany has 22 local bird clubs across 16 regions. See every German club by region.

NABU BirdLife in Germany, with reserve information, identification guides and the Blumberger Muehle centre above. Visit Dachverband Deutscher Avifaunisten The umbrella body for German bird monitoring, and the source behind most national population figures. Visit Kranichschutz Deutschland The crane conservation partnership behind the Kranorama hide and the counts on the Bodden. Visit ornitho.de The national recording portal, run by the DDA with the state ornithological societies. Visit Institut fuer Vogelforschung, Vogelwarte Helgoland The Helgoland bird observatory. It has ringed since 1910, and it is the reason the island migration record exists. Visit
